How does an optical probe read a smart water meter?

Fig 1 · Reading the meter

    The bits of the letter on the light right now. Light on = 0, dark = 1, so the line rests dark. Each letter: start bit, 7 data bits, a parity bit that keeps the count of 1s even, and a stop bit.

    Meter colour

    The big idea: the probe is a serial cable whose wire is a beam of invisible light.

    Where the numbers come from
    • Mode C conversation (300 baud sign-on /?!, the meter's identification with its speed letter, the acknowledgement ␆0Z0, then data at the new speed) and the BCC rule (XOR of every byte after STX up to and including ETX): IEC 62056-21, as summarised in the OpenMUC j62056 guide and Ipesoft D2000 docs.
    • 300 baud, 7 data bits, even parity, 1 stop bit at sign-on: reported from real meters on the MySensors forum. 10 bits per letter gives 33.3 ms per letter at 300 baud and 1.04 ms at 9600.
    • 200 ms: the meter's minimum reaction time before it answers (Ipesoft docs, quoting the standard).
    • Light on = 0, dark = 1, so the line rests dark: how DIY read heads wire the LED and sensor to a UART; check it against the standard's optical clause before you rely on it.
    • 940 nm: typical of these probes' LEDs (product listings, e.g. this one on Tindie, give ~900 nm send and 800–1000 nm receive).
    • 8-0:1.0.0: OBIS medium 8 is water (IEC 62056-6-1, see ITWissen). The rest of the code, the maker WPA, the serial and the total are invented for this figure. Your meter's manual lists its real registers.
    • The probe is drawn after the MY015-D: a magnetic cup about 34 mm across with an LED and a sensor side by side, and an FT232 USB-to-serial chip in its USB-C plug.
